tagline: Position in the periodic table, the two kinds of hydride, water and hydrogen peroxide.

overview.intro: Hydrogen fits nowhere comfortably: it resembles the alkali metals in holding one electron and the halogens in needing one more, and it is placed above group 1 while behaving unlike any member of it. The chapter covers that dual personality, the classification of hydrides into ionic, covalent and metallic types, the preparation and properties of water including its hard and soft forms, and the structure, preparation, strength as an oxidant and decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. Peroxide calculations are the most common numerical in this unit, so the ratio arithmetic is worked through explicitly.

learningOutcomes: Explain the anomalous position of hydrogen and its resemblance to both group 1 and group 17.
Classify hydrides as ionic, covalent or metallic and give two examples of each.
Describe the preparation, structure and properties of water and distinguish hard from soft water.
Describe the preparation, structure and reactions of hydrogen peroxide, including its oxidising and reducing behaviour.
Solve volumetric and strength problems involving hydrogen peroxide as a titre and as an oxidant.

learn.title: Hydrogen, its isotopes and the hydride family

blocks.text: Hydrogen has a single electron in a 1s orbital, which gives it the group 1 character of forming a +1 ion, but its small size and high ionisation energy make it behave unlike the alkali metals: it forms covalent bonds rather than metallic ones and is a non-metal. It also needs one electron to reach the helium configuration, exactly as the halogens do, which explains its placement above group 1 with a note of its dual nature. When hydrogen reacts with metals it gains an electron to form the hydride ion H−, giving ionic or saline hydrides such as sodium hydride; with non-metals it shares electrons to give covalent hydrides such as methane and ammonia; and with the transition and inner-transition metals it forms metallic or interstitial hydrides, where hydrogen atoms occupy holes in the metal lattice and the alloys can absorb enormous volumes of hydrogen.

items: Three isotopes: protium with no neutron, deuterium with one, tritium with two and radioactivity.
Ionic hydrides contain H− and come from s-block metals; they liberate hydrogen on contact with water.
Covalent hydrides are discrete molecules of the p-block elements and the basis of organic chemistry.
Metallic hydrides form with d- and f-block metals and are non-stoichiometric, such as LaH2.8.
Hydrogen resembles lithium in forming a monoxide and forming only weakly basic solutions.
Like the halogens it forms a negative ion, has high electronegativity for a non-metal and needs one electron for a full shell.

items.note: The hydride ion is a strong base and deprotonates water immediately.

items.text: Palladium absorbing many hundred times its own volume of hydrogen
items.note: Hydrogen atoms occupy interstices, giving an interstitial metallic hydride used for storage.

blocks.text: Water is a bent molecule with a bond angle of 104.5°, and because oxygen is far more electronegative than hydrogen the bond dipoles reinforce rather than cancel. Each molecule can form four hydrogen bonds, two through its lone pairs and two through its hydrogens, and this tetrahedral network explains nearly every anomaly: the high boiling point for a molecule of its mass, the density maximum at 4 °C that lets ice float and keeps lakes alive in winter, and the high surface tension that supports insects. In the laboratory water is prepared by burning hydrogen in excess oxygen or by removing dissolved gases through prolonged boiling. Hardness comes from dissolved calcium and magnesium salts: temporary hardness is caused by hydrogencarbonates and is removed by boiling, while permanent hardness comes from sulphates and chlorides and needs washing soda or ion exchange.

items: Water is amphoteric: it ionises as an acid to give H3O+ and as a base to accept a proton.
Temporary hardness is removed by boiling: Ca(HCO3)2 → CaCO3 + CO2 + H2O.
Permanent hardness requires washing soda, which precipitates calcium as carbonate, or a cation-exchange resin.
Soap lathers poorly with hard water because calcium and magnesium stearates precipitate as scum.
Ice floats because the hydrogen-bonded lattice holds molecules further apart than the liquid does.

items.text: Adding washing soda to hard water
items.note: Na2CO3 + CaSO4 → CaCO3 + Na2SO4, removing the calcium as an insoluble carbonate.

items.text: Passing hard water through a sodium-zeolite resin
items.note: Calcium ions are retained and sodium ions released, softening the water and regenerating with brine.

items.meaning: Hardness caused by hydrogencarbonates of calcium and magnesium, removable by boiling.
Hardness caused by sulphates and chlorides of calcium and magnesium.
Ion exchange in which hard-water cations are swapped for sodium ions.
Self-ionisation of water into H3O+ and OH−, giving Kw.

learn.title: Hydrogen peroxide: structure, preparation and reactions

blocks.text: Hydrogen peroxide has an open-book structure: two O–H bonds at an angle to the O–O bond, with a dihedral angle of about 90° in the gas phase because the lone pairs on adjacent oxygens repel each other. It is prepared in the laboratory by treating sodium peroxide with ice-cold dilute hydrochloric acid, or by the electrolytic oxidation of sulphuric acid, and it is stored in dark waxed bottles with stabilisers because it decomposes slowly to water and oxygen, faster in light and in the presence of dust. Its chemistry is dominated by the oxidation state of oxygen, which is −1 in peroxide and can move either way: with stronger oxidants it behaves as a reducing agent, giving up oxygen, and with mild reductants it acts as an oxidising agent, accepting electrons to reach the stable −2 state. That ambivalence makes it useful as a bleach, an antiseptic and a rocket propellant.

items: Structure: non-planar, O–O single bond 1.48 Å with O–H bonds inclined about 97°.
Preparation: Na2O2 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O2, kept cold to limit decomposition.
Decomposition: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2, catalysed by manganese dioxide, light and traces of alkali.
As an oxidant in acid: H2O2 + 2H+ + 2e− → 2H2O, the permanganate titration reaction.
As a reductant: H2O2 → O2 + 2H+ + 2e−, decolourising acidified potassium manganate(VII).
Its bleaching action is oxidation of coloured matter, unlike sulphur dioxide which is reduction.

items.text: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) is decolourised by peroxide
items.note: 2KMnO4 + 5H2O2 + 3H2SO4 → 2MnSO4 + K2SO4 + 5O2 + 8H2O, showing peroxide as the reductant.
Cr2O7^2− turns green as peroxide reduces chromium(VI), forming the blue peroxo complex first.

learn.title: Strength, volume and titration arithmetic for peroxide

blocks.text: Peroxide questions come in two forms. The volumetric form uses the equivalent relationship between potassium manganate(VII) and hydrogen peroxide in acidic solution: one mole of permanganate accepts five electrons while one mole of peroxide releases two, giving a mole ratio of 2 : 5. The strength form converts a concentration into grams per litre by multiplying by the molar mass of H2O2, which is 34, and the volume-strength relationship 22.4 L of oxygen at STP per litre of solution is the standard check: a solution labelled 11.2 volume contains 34 g per litre because one litre liberates 11.2 L of oxygen, half a mole. Reading the label correctly and applying the 2 : 5 ratio are the only two skills these questions demand.

items: One litre of x volume H2O2 liberates x litres of oxygen at STP.
Strength in g L^-1 = volume strength × 1.7, since 22.4 L of O2 corresponds to 34 g of H2O2.
Titration ratio 2KMnO4 : 5H2O2 in acidic medium.
Molarity = strength in g L^-1 ÷ 34.
Always state the medium: acidic permanganate oxidises peroxide, alkaline permanganate does not.

items.note: One litre gives 11.2 L of O2 at STP, which is 0.5 mol, so the sample holds 0.5 mol × 34 = 17 g L^-1.

items.text: 20 mL of 0.1 M KMnO4 against peroxide
items.note: Moles permanganate = 0.002, so moles peroxide = 0.002 × 5/2 = 0.005 in the aliquot.

items.meaning: Litres of oxygen at STP liberated by one litre of the peroxide solution.
Molar mass divided by the number of electrons transferred in the reaction.
Apparent charge on an atom, −1 for oxygen in peroxides.
Volumetric determination of an unknown concentration using a standard solution.

keyPoints: Hydrogen has one electron in 1s and shows resemblance to both group 1 and group 17.
Isotopes protium, deuterium and tritium differ only in neutron count.
Ionic hydrides contain H−, covalent hydrides are molecular, metallic hydrides store hydrogen in the lattice.
Water is bent at 104.5° and hydrogen-bonded, giving a boiling point far above its mass predicts.
Ice floats because its open hydrogen-bonded lattice is less dense than the liquid.
Temporary hardness is removed by boiling; permanent hardness needs washing soda or ion exchange.
Hydrogen peroxide has a non-planar open-book structure with oxygen in the −1 oxidation state.
H2O2 decomposes to water and oxygen, catalysed by light, dust and manganese dioxide.
With strong oxidants peroxide is a reductant; with mild reductants it is an oxidant.
Volume strength × 1.7 gives strength in g L^-1; the titration ratio with permanganate is 5 : 2.
examFocus: In hydride questions, name the family first, then give the example and its characteristic reaction.
Water questions reward the structure: hydrogen bonding for the boiling point, the open lattice for the density anomaly.
For peroxide, decide the role from the partner: permanganate means peroxide is the reductant, iodide means it is the oxidant.
Volume-strength arithmetic works in two steps: oxygen volume to moles, moles to grams using 34 g mol^-1.

vocabulary.meaning: Binary compound of hydrogen with another element.
Ionic hydride of an s-block metal containing the H− ion.
Hydrogen atoms trapped in the holes of a metal lattice.
Hardness from hydrogencarbonates, removed by boiling.
Hardness from sulphates or chlorides, needing chemical treatment.
Able to act as either an acid or a base, as water does.
Apparent charge on an atom, taken as −1 for oxygen in peroxides.
Litres of oxygen at STP given by one litre of hydrogen peroxide solution.
Removal of colour, achieved by oxidation with peroxide or reduction with sulphur dioxide.
The elemental form H2, a colourless odourless gas and the lightest of all substances.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen differs from the other elements of group 1 because:
options: It is a non-metal and forms covalent bonds rather than metallic ones
questions.answer: It is a non-metal and forms covalent bonds rather than metallic ones
questions.explanation: Its tiny size and single electron give high ionisation energy, so it shares electrons instead of forming a metallic lattice.

questions.prompt: The hydride formed when sodium reacts with hydrogen is:
questions.explanation: Sodium transfers its electron to hydrogen, giving Na+ and the saline hydride ion H−.

questions.prompt: Temporary hardness in water is caused by and removed by:
options: Hydrogencarbonates of calcium and magnesium, by boiling
Chlorides of sodium, by adding washing soda
questions.answer: Hydrogencarbonates of calcium and magnesium, by boiling
questions.explanation: Boiling decomposes the hydrogencarbonates to insoluble carbonates, while sulphates and chlorides survive boiling.

questions.prompt: When hydrogen peroxide is added to acidified potassium manganate(VII), the peroxide acts as:
options: An oxidising agent and is reduced to water
A reducing agent and is oxidised to oxygen
A catalyst that is not consumed
questions.answer: A reducing agent and is oxidised to oxygen
questions.explanation: Permanganate is the stronger oxidant, so peroxide donates oxygen, releases electrons and is itself oxidised to O2.

questions.prompt: The three isotopes of hydrogen are protium, deuterium and __________ .
questions.explanation: Tritium has two neutrons and is radioactive, with a half-life of about 12.3 years.

questions.prompt: One litre of a hydrogen peroxide solution of strength x volume liberates x litres of __________ at standard conditions.
questions.explanation: Volume strength is defined by the oxygen evolved at STP from one litre of the solution.

questions.prompt: Explain in what ways hydrogen resembles both group 1 and group 17.
questions.answer: Like group 1 it has one valence electron, shows oxidation state +1 in compounds such as HCl and forms a monoxide. Like group 17 it needs one electron to complete its shell, forms a univalent negative ion H− in ionic hydrides, and has high electronegativity for a non-metal. Its small size explains why it is a non-metal rather than an alkali metal.
questions.explanation: The single electron gives both resemblances; size decides which behaviour dominates.

questions.prompt: Describe two laboratory methods of preparing hydrogen peroxide.
questions.answer: First, ice-cold dilute hydrochloric acid is added to sodium peroxide, giving sodium chloride and peroxide, which is filtered and stored in dark bottles. Second, the electrolytic oxidation of sulphuric acid produces peroxydisulphuric acid, which is hydrolysed to give hydrogen peroxide. Low temperature throughout prevents decomposition.
questions.explanation: Both methods avoid heat and alkali because peroxide decomposes readily under those conditions.

questions.prompt: Explain why hydrogen peroxide can act as both an oxidising agent and a reducing agent, and give one example of each role.
questions.answer: In hydrogen peroxide oxygen has the oxidation state −1, intermediate between the zero of O2 and the −2 of water and oxides. It can therefore move in either direction: when it meets a stronger oxidising agent such as acidified potassium manganate(VII) it loses electrons, rises to oxidation state 0 in oxygen and acts as a reductant, decolourising the permanganate. When it meets a mild reducing agent such as potassium iodide it accepts electrons, falls to −2 in water and acts as an oxidant, liberating brown iodine. The intermediate oxidation state is what makes both roles possible.
questions.explanation: An intermediate oxidation state permits oxidation and reduction; the role adopted depends on the strength of the partner.

questions.prompt: A sample of hydrogen peroxide solution is labelled 11.2 volume. Calculate its strength in grams per litre and its molarity.
questions.answer: One litre of the solution liberates 11.2 L of oxygen at STP, which is 11.2/22.4 = 0.5 mol of O2. The decomposition 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2 shows that one mole of oxygen comes from two moles of peroxide, so 0.5 mol O2 requires 1.0 mol of H2O2, which is 34 g. The strength is therefore 34 g L^-1, and the molarity is 34/34 = 1.0 M.
questions.explanation: Convert the volume strength to moles of oxygen first, double it for peroxide using the 2 : 1 stoichiometry, then convert to mass.
